articles.sourceTitle: Why is AI generated language so hard to understand?
articles.title: [2610.29162] Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?
articles.text:
Computer Science > Computation and Language

arXiv:2610.29162 (cs)

Title:Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?

View a PDF of the paper titled Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?, by Thomas Hikaru Clark and 2 other authors
View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract:There is a widespread sense that AI-generated text has recently become harder to understand. In this study, we investigate a set of psycholinguistic features that are known to correlate with human processing difficulty (e.g., object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies, low-frequency n-grams). Using a novel corpus of AI-generated text across diverse domains, we find that AI models use these difficult features more often than paraphrases generated by round-trip translation. Compared with human writing, all nine frontier and near-frontier models use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams, and most also use longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation; we also demonstrate substantial variation across model families. We propose and test a hypothesis as to why: while human language is optimized for successful communication, AI-generated text is increasingly optimized for other goals like math, code, and reasoning, in which there is a pressure for \textit{information density} rather than successful communication. We provide a proof-of-concept for this hypothesis by fine-tuning a language model under a length penalty, which leads to a divergence from human-like linguistic behavior. Our findings highlight the axes of misalignment between linguistic processing demands in humans and LLMs, and point toward possible remedies.

articles.title: How Cerebras Deploys Trillion-Parameter AI Models
articles.text: One of the most frequently asked questions we get is how we deploy large models on Cerebras wafer-scale chips. A single Cerebras WSE-3T wafer has 44 GB of on-chip memory, and trillion-parameter frontier models need terabytes for their weights alone.In this post, we’ll explain how we split a large frontier model across multiple WSE-3T wafers, to run multi-trillion parameter models at 1000-2000+ tokens per second.We’ll use the open source model Kimi K3, with ~3 trillion parameters, as an illustrative example.By the end, you'll understand:How we fit the full model into on-chip memoryHow we map the model across multiple chipsHow we handle a high # of concurrent requestsBreaking it down with Kimi K3Kimi K3 is an open source, 3T parameter model with 69 linear-attention layers and 24 dense layers.For this illustrative example, we use:A 256k assumed average request size4-bit weight quantization (like the Hugging Face implementation)An 8-bit KV cache#1: Size of Each layerTo calculate the total number of Cerebras WSE-3T wafers we need to support Kimi K3, let’s first calculate the size of each model layer.Kimi K3 has 3 trillion parameters. If all 3T parameters are stored at 4 bits each, the raw parameter payload is:Dividing that payload by 93 layers then gives:#2: Number of WafersNow that we know each layer needs about 16 GB, we can figure out how many layers fit on each 44 GB wafer. The answer depends on the layer type:Dense layers need additional room for a KV cache, because each dense (full-attention) layer stores the keys and values for every token in every active request. So, we place one dense layer per wafer and leave the remaining SRAM for its KV cache.Linear-attention layers do not require additional room for a KV cache. Instead of storing keys and values for every token, a linear-attention layer keeps a small, fixed-size state per request, regardless of context length. That leaves room for two linear layers per wafer (2 × 16 GB = 32 GB).Therefore, with Kimi K3’s 69 linear layers and 24 dense layers, we get:This gives us a total wafer count of 35 + 24 = 59 wafers.#3: Connecting the wafers togetherCerebras executes models in a pipeline. After the Cerebras compiler maps the model layers across regions of wafers, the runtime maps the path for tokens to flow between wafers. For ultrafast latency, only activations need to be passed between the wafers, and this can be done via RDMA over Ethernet. This is roughly 2 microseconds per hop.It’s important to emphasize that because each Cerebras wafer has 44 GB of on-chip SRAM and each layer is only 16 GB, we are typically able to fit entire layers of the model directly on the chip.This means that in most cases, the model weights never have to move, and layers don’t need to be split across wafers. Only activations cross from one wafer to the next.#4: How we serve 1 requestNow that we have our wafers connected together and the model laid out, we can think of each wafer as one stage in an assembly line: the model’s weights for each stage stay in place, and the request’s intermediate results move through the layer stages.For example, Wafer 1 runs model layers 1–2 and sends its activations to wafer 2. Wafer 2 runs layers 3–4 and passes its results to Wafer 3, and so on until the last wafer produces the next token.#5: How we serve many requestsThis raises a common misconception. If a token has to travel through each wafer in order, doesn’t each wafer sit idle while it waits for its turn? In effect, wouldn't the system be running at a batch size of one?No! If we only sent one request down the line at a time and waited for it to complete before starting the next request, this would be an inefficient use of the pipeline. Instead, we keep the entire pipeline full with different requests. Because the model is split into pipeline stages already, each stage can work on a different request at the same time.While stage 3 processes a token for request A, stage 2 processes one for request B, and stage 1 one for request C. In our example, each stage is a layer. In production, Cerebras uses much finer-grained stages, and many more of them.Each stage can also process a micro-batch, a small group of requests, rather than a single request. So the number of requests in flight is roughly the number of stages times the micro-batch size.To understand the tradeoff, smaller micro-batches make each request even faster, while larger micro-batches increase total throughput.#6: How many requests can we serve?The amount of on-chip memory allocated to KV cache determines the maximum number of concurrent requests. Every request in flight needs its own KV cache on each dense-layer wafer, so the size of on-chip memory sets the ceiling on concurrent requests. As explained above, we only need to calculate KV cache requirements for dense layers.For each 44 GB wafer that already has one dense layer, we can calculate the remaining space for the KV cache with:Total wafer storage - size of one dense layer. In this case:Calculating the # of Concurrent RequestsTo find the number of concurrent requests supported for any particular model mapping, we first calculate how much cache a single 256k request takes up:To then calculate the total number of concurrent requests this configuration would support, we divide:The total number of concurrent requests represents the number of simultaneous requests moving through the pipeline at any point in time. Unlike a GPU batch, those requests don’t wait for one another to finish, they stream through the pipeline continuously.Of course, neither concurrency nor batch size tells you exactly how efficiently an inference system performs. When evaluating the throughput of an inference system, the more meaningful metric is total token throughput per unit of power (e.g. tokens per second per megawatt), when measured at the same output generation speed.How this scales beyond 3T parametersThe same approach extends to larger models: calculate the memory needed for weights and request state, distribute the model across wafers, and connect them into a pipeline. Each additional wafer contributes compute and on-chip memory, allowing us to accommodate models that exceed the capacity of any single chip.Thanks for learning with us! Interested in deploying a model on Cerebras or building with our inference cloud?Get started with our free API: cloud.cerebras.aiReach out to our sales team: sales@cerebras.aiDesigns by Halley Chang. articles.title: GitHub - slee-persis/GVS5H: GVS5H: Five Qwen3.8-27B Models Match Claude Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard | Fable 5 Level Coding for a Fifth the Price
articles.text:
GVS5H: Five Qwen3.8-27B Models Match Claude Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard
GVS5H: Gorilla vs. 5 Humans

Opus 5 ran on an earlier version of the scaffold, in a single pass served through OpenRouter rather than five on a pinned backend.

Abstract. Frontier coding performance is typically bought with larger proprietary models at high cost. We introduce ledger-based zero-shot self-orchestration, a training-free method in which fresh instances of one model decompose problems and coordinate through a shared filesystem holding a plan, notes and current solution. Across eleven open and closed-weight models on the 100 latest hard LiveCodeBench problems, the method yields gains of up to 25.6 percentage points on pinned backends and offers two routes to frontier-level accuracy. Orchestrated Qwen3.8 Flash Next reaches 93.0% pass@1 against Fable 5's 90.4% at 9% of the cost, and locally served, open-weight Qwen3.8-27B rises from 66.8% to 92.4%. Gains are not universal: some models are unchanged or worse. Transcript analysis attributes the gain to decomposition and persistent context. Inference-time organization can approach frontier coding accuracy at a fraction of the cost, or slightly exceed it on self-hostable weights.
— the paper

Needs uv and an API key for the model you want to test.
cd codebase/v2-current
export OPENAI_API_KEY=...

LCB_RELEASE=release_v6 \
ESCALATION_CLOUD_MAX_TOKENS=128000 \
ESCALATION_CLOUD_TIMEOUT=7200 \
MULTIAGENT_MODEL=openai:gpt-5.6-terra \
uv run --no-project --python 3.12 --with 'datasets<4' --with numpy --with anthropic \
python escalation/run_bench.py --engine multiagent --only lcb --lcb 100 --parallel 8

--engine multiagent runs the manager; --engine single is the one-call baseline.
Other models: anthropic:<model>, dashscope:<model>, openrouter:<model>, each with its own *_API_KEY.
The pass@1 score prints at the end. Results are written to runs/results.json, workspaces to runs/ws/.

articles.sourceTitle: Nikon photography contest winner loses title after scientists spot signs of AI
articles.title: Nikon photography contest winner loses title after scientists spot telltale signs of AI-generated footage
articles.text:
A hot potato: It seems that the once-popular trend of entering AI-generated content in competitions made for humans hasn't gone away. The winner of one of the world's most prestigious scientific photography awards has just had his title stripped from him after his entry was determined to have been created using AI.

Nikon's 16th annual Small World in Motion contest is open to any movie or digital time-lapse photography taken through the microscope.
This year's winner was Dr. Ning Xu, from Tsinghua University in China, whose video captured tiny cilia beating in the airways of a child with primary ciliary dyskinesia, a rare respiratory disorder.

But Xu's entry raised several concerns among members of the scientific community. Some researchers said there were abnormalities in the structure and size of the cells and that their features appeared and disappeared in a way not seen in cellular biology.
One associate professor at the University of Florida said some of the structures "pop in and out of existence" and the cilia "appear from nowhere," which are classic indications that a video was AI-generated.

A more damning discovery came from PhD student Ian Donovan at UT Southwestern Medical Center, who said the source image appeared to contain a distinctive watermark indicating it had been AI-generated. Two former competition judges also raised concerns about the clip's legitimacy.
In a now-deleted LinkedIn post, Xu admitted to using AI in the video, but he said it was only used to "distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images from the super-resolution optical imaging" during post-processing.
He added that AI had not been used to generate the video itself, the cilia, or their movement.
Xu insists that he has not broken competition rules. While enhancing the visibility of microscopic structures is common and allowed, researchers typically use techniques such as applying stains and dyes to the samples themselves.
However, Xu's explanation doesn't account for the abnormalities found in his video. Some scientists said the doubts could have been removed if Xu had shared the RAW grayscale video.
An investigation by Nikon found that Xu had violated the competition's rules, and he was subsequently stripped of his prize. The top spot has instead been awarded to Nguyen Nam Nhat of Vietnam, who entered a video of a tiny roundworm and a single-celled organism.
Following the incident, Nikon said in a statement that it plans to "revisit rules and evaluation procedures for future competition entries."
We've seen several examples of AI-generated images being entered into, and sometimes winning, art competitions going back years. A Midjourney image won a category in Colorado State Fair's annual art competition in 2022, while another creation won a photography contest hosted by Australian photo retailer digiDirect in 2023.
There was also the case of an artist who won a category in the 2023 Sony World Photography Awards but refused his prize because his image (below) was AI-generated – something that seems quite obvious these days.

In a more satisfying story from 2024, a man who won a digital art competition using an AI-generated image and was thoroughly unapologetic about it complained that people had started stealing his "work" and he couldn't copyright it.
